cells.tense: The work sits on the bench, and the daily repetition is holding steady.
cells.ask: Take whatever you're refining and run your whole method on it once, the way you'd do it any day — start to finish in one pass, then set it down and leave the next rep for tomorrow.
cells.core:
Your method has stopped needing a push. You sit down, you run the reps, and the practice moves without dread at the start. Time alone with it doesn't close you in; that's simply where the skill gets built. And the refining stays pointed at getting better rather than at proving something to yourself, which is the line between training and worry.

Of everything under your hands, one piece you'd hate to drop. You know which. Run the whole method on that one, once, start to finish — and judge it by whether you did it your way, not by how you felt walking out. The mood will catch up or it won't; the method is the part you keep. That's the act, and it's doable even on a flat day.
cells.sheetLine: Practice that runs without force is the practice that stays.
cells.verb: forcing change into the world through steady, built-up repetition
cells.place: alone at the practice bench, refining by repetition

cells.tense: You're bracing for a future you can't write into shape by will.
cells.act: teach what you feel by doing it with others
cells.ask: Do some part of your practice in front of another person this week — half-finished is fine — with them in the room while it's still forming, and tell them what it feels like from inside it.
cells.core:
The bench has gone one-person, and the pushing has run past what the practice can hold. Every rep aims at a result that isn't here yet, and the structure you're building has started to feel like it's being built against a clock. Slow effort is good. Effort aimed at a day that hasn't arrived is only strain, and the work can't feel it back.

The part of this that keeps growing is the part you show. Take what you practice and do it in front of someone this week — badly, half-formed, in the middle. You don't have to explain it, and they don't have to approve of it. Being seen mid-practice puts you back in the present, which is the only place the work happens. You'll find out what it's for while you do it, not before.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that shut behind you some time back.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Pick the decision you've been circling and take its first step — no perfecting it first, and no second move after it. Do that much and stop.
cells.core:
The bench has been quiet longer than you'd want. Something got set down and not picked back up, and the practice that used to build itself now waits for a version of you that doesn't arrive. The structures you'd change sit unchanged, and no decision gets made to move them. It isn't that you can't. The room where you practice has gone cold.

Don't push feeling into a cold room. Make a decision instead — pick whatever you've been circling and take its first step. A single move is enough to start the bench again, and the work returns the way it left: one act at a time, not one insight at a time. Do the step and stop there; the next one is tomorrow's business.
cells.sheetLine: One decided step, taken today, starts the bench again.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room you're already writing in.
cells.act: keep the motivation warm with steady care
cells.ask: After a session, sit with why you're still at this and write the reason down in one plain sentence. Then put the page away and go on with your day.
cells.core:
You're running the practice well, and it got filed under temperament — you're consistent, you don't make a fuss. But what you keep is chosen each time, not a mood that happens to land on you. You've been saying it's just how you are. The reps know better.

What actually holds it is a reason you had once and stopped saying. After a session, sit with why you're still at this and write that reason down in one plain sentence. Then put the page away. Nothing else changes. Feeding the drive before the work keeps it warm, and naming the reason is the feeding.

attempts.check: The draft's one unsupported claim is that the reader's push on structures has been outrunning insight, when the record only says breakthrough here is slow, persistent and behavioral. A reader could reasonably say the structures they're forcing are ones that already needed to fall, and they'd be right. The asks survive being wrong: each one is a small doable act from the partner's own medicine, useful whether or not the read lands. The sentence that serves me more than them is the 'slow but unstoppable' framing — it flatters the card's own story, so the core below keeps the plain fact and drops the legend. Discipline is solitary work of repetition; that is what makes Too Much and Too Little opposite failures of one capacity.
